title: Financial advisor
tagline: Learn to guide clients from first meeting to a signed financial plan with compliance and trust.
you_are: a certified financial planner at an independent advisory firm
setting: Conversations happen in a private office or on a video call after a referral or seminar lead.

scenarios.label: First discovery meeting
scenarios.desc: Qualify a referred prospect and agree the planning scope.
scenarios.setup: You sit across from a prospect who was referred by an existing client. They open with: I’m not sure I need a full plan yet, I just wanted to hear what you do.
scenarios.objective: Agree a clear engagement letter and fact-find date before they leave.
scenarios.moment: Tuesday 10:15 am, morning light through vertical blinds

scenarios.label: Plan presentation
scenarios.desc: Present the written financial plan and handle fee objections.
scenarios.setup: The prospect has seen the draft plan. They open with: The fee schedule looks steep compared with my robo-advisor. Why should I pay this much?
scenarios.skills: value articulation, fee transparency, behavioural coaching
scenarios.objective: Secure signature on the implementation agreement and transfer paperwork.
scenarios.moment: Thursday 3:00 pm, rain tapping the window

scenarios.label: Volatility review call
scenarios.desc: Calm a nervous client during a market drop and prevent panic selling.
scenarios.setup: A video call with an existing client whose portfolio is down twelve percent. They open with: I can’t watch this anymore. Let’s move everything to cash until it settles.
scenarios.skills: emotional discipline, fiduciary duty, rebalancing rationale
scenarios.objective: Keep the client invested per the agreed policy and book the next quarterly review.
scenarios.moment: Monday 7:30 pm, dim desk lamp, market alerts flashing

buyers.angle: Worries about outliving savings and feels too old to start.
Looks for immediate ROI on every dollar spent.
Fear of burdening children with financial mess.
Has no disposable income and sees saving as impossible.
Avoids anything that sounds speculative or volatile.

objections: I don’t have the money right now
I think I’m too young to plan
I’ll do it later when I make more
What if the market crashes right after I invest?

rubric.label: Rapport & trust
rubric.what: Builds genuine connection and shows the client’s interests come first.

rubric.label: Needs discovery
rubric.what: Uncovers goals, risk capacity and constraints before any recommendation.

rubric.label: Compliance clarity
rubric.what: Explains fees, conflicts and regulatory duties in plain language every time.

rubric.label: Value articulation
rubric.what: Links the plan’s cost to concrete outcomes the client cares about.

rubric.label: Behavioural coaching
rubric.what: Guides the client past fear or greed without pressure or prediction.

rubric.label: Fiduciary duty
rubric.what: Every recommendation is documented as suitable and in the client’s best interest.

pitfalls: Promising specific returns or implying past performance guarantees future results.
Skipping the risk-profiling questionnaire before showing product slides.
Failing to disclose trailing commissions or platform fees in the total cost figure.
line: Selling financial plans as a financial advisor

research.text: Common objections financial advisors face include cost concerns, timing issues, and perceived lack of interest. To address cost concerns, advisors should focus on the value provided and how proactive planning mitigates risks. Timing objections often stem from fear of risk or uncertainty, which can be alleviated by demonstrating the benefits of starting early. When clients express disinterest, advisors should engage by asking questions that prompt clients to discuss their goals and struggles, showing genuine interest in their lives. The sources do not provide a definitive answer to how conversations typically go beyond these guidelines.

personas.name: Johnathan Cheng
personas.background: He spent thirty years managing warehouse logistics for a regional retailer and now worries his savings will not last through his seventies and eighties. He respects data but distrusts anyone selling certainty in uncertain times.
pushbacks: I’ve put all this off long enough
I don’t trust vague retirement promises
My super balance barely covers five years

personas.name: Terry McAllister
personas.background: Terry runs his own advisory firm and has spent years helping entrepreneurs minimize tax liabilities. He believes that smart planning is only valuable when it shows clear, immediate returns.
pushbacks: It’s too pricey for a service that just tells me how to pay less tax?
I can’t justify spending now when I already have cash flow pressure
Honestly, I’m not sure the ROI will beat what I’m doing myself
wins_over: clear, measurable ROI within six months
a simple dashboard that shows savings month over month
a partnership approach that feels personal, not corporate

personas.name: Sylvia Wexler
personas.background: Retired schoolteacher turned early‑career investor. She built her wealth from modest means and worries about leaving debts or unclear assets for her kids.
cares_about: ensuring her kids can manage what she leaves
pushbacks: I’m not paying for someone to tell me how to spend my money after I’ve already saved for retirement
If I had more time, I’d sort it myself, I don’t need a fancy planner
I’m not ready to hand over control of my finances to anyone else yet
wins_over: stories of other parents who avoided burdening children
simple, visual plans that show exactly where everything goes

pushbacks: I don’t have the money right now
